spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: Scaling t=nτ and applying Stirling compress the n-dependence into an exponential phase f and a slower amplitude g. Expanding the trigonometric factor into finitely many frequencies then turns one contour integral into a family of saddle problems indexed by λ.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: After the contour representation is scaled and its gamma factors are treated by Stirling's formula, the source writes the integral in phase-amplitude form e^{nf(τ)}g(τ) on a specified cut plane. A recurrence shows sin^b(z)cot_b(z)=V_b(cos z), permitting a finite decomposition into integrals J_{n,λ} with phase f(τ)−λπiτ. Their stationary equation is f′(τ)=λπi and is related to an algebraic polynomial in τ.
directed.conceptual_reading: Phase-amplitude separation isolates exponential growth from prefactors, while frequency decomposition converts oscillation into a parameter shift of the phase. The hard asymptotic question is thereby reduced to locating and comparing finitely many admissible critical points.
directed.representation_or_bridge: Gamma-product asymptotics bridge the rational-function contour to a Laplace-type integral; the polynomial V_b bridges the cotangent factor to frequency-indexed integrals; exponentiating the saddle equation bridges analytic stationarity to polynomial root geometry.
directed.boundary_or_failure: This reduction does not prove that the proposed contour deformations are valid, that saddles are unique, or which frequency dominates. Branch choices and cut geometry remain part of those proof burdens.

spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: The decisive step is not merely finding stationary points but organizing them on a closed level curve so contours can pass through the correct saddles and their real phase values can be ordered. Under the root-separation condition, that geometry reduces the full frequency sum to the outer admissible contributions that set the exponential rate.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: Assuming condition (19), Lemma 4 classifies the solutions of f′(τ)=λπi in the right half-plane and places them on the closed curve Re(f′)=0 with a stated inside/outside sign rule. Contours are deformed through the corresponding saddles, and Laplace's method gives |J_{n,λ}| in terms of exp(n Re(f_0(τ_λ))). Lemma 6 uses monotonicity of Re(f_0) along the curve to select the relevant extreme frequencies and obtains the exponential rate κ of I_n.
directed.conceptual_reading: Saddle geometry supplies a selection principle: critical points are not interchangeable, and their ordering along a constrained curve determines which exponential contribution survives at scale n. This turns a finite decomposition into one controlling rate.
directed.representation_or_bridge: Polynomial roots encode the saddles, the level curve encodes their global arrangement, admissible contour deformations localize each integral, and Laplace asymptotics translate the selected saddle's phase into κ.
directed.boundary_or_failure: The conclusion depends on condition (19), uniqueness and admissibility of the listed saddles, and the contour geometry. It only supplies the analytic size budget; it does not itself compare that rate with denominators or coefficient growth. For b>1 the stated result is a limsup rather than an ordinary limit.
directed.uncertainty: The qualitative selection mechanism is recoverable, but damaged radicals, contour coordinates, exponents, conjugation typography, and the exact root condition require typeset-source verification.

spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: Coefficient size has its own saddle problem. Elementary derivative bounds give a coarse exponential budget, but auxiliary horizontal integrals exposing the coefficients allow a sharper rate governed by the nearest imaginary polynomial root, distinct from the saddle controlling smallness of the original linear form.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: Bounds on the partial-fraction derivatives B_{k,j}, relations expressing A_s through them, and Stirling's formula yield Lemma 7's uniform exponential upper bound for the rational coefficients. The source then represents certain horizontal integrals as linear combinations of A_{b+2},…,A_{a+b−1}; gamma asymptotics and saddle analysis sharpen the bound in Lemma 8 to Re(f_0(η)), where η is an imaginary root of the same polynomial with minimal modulus. Equality is stated for the highest indexed coefficient.
directed.conceptual_reading: The construction separates usefulness from cost: one saddle regime controls decay of the linear form, whereas another controls growth of the coefficients needed to express it. The final criterion must compare these distinct geometric measurements rather than treating one asymptotic as sufficient.
directed.representation_or_bridge: Partial-fraction coefficients first give a combinatorial bound; auxiliary integrals then bridge selected A_s to a contour representation whose imaginary saddle yields a sharper common exponential rate.
directed.boundary_or_failure: The sharpened estimate is conditional on the root hypothesis and bounds coefficient growth only. It does not establish denominator integrality, linear-form decay, or the final independence inequality, and most coefficients receive an upper bound rather than an exact asymptotic.
directed.uncertainty: Derivative powers, factorial ratios, integral powers, root notation, and rate exponents are corrupted in places; exact numerical or symbolic use requires checking the PDF.

spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: The proof closes by treating arithmetic saving, linear-form decay, and coefficient growth as tunable exponential budgets. Parameter choices are successful only when their combined rate crosses a strict negativity threshold, after which the same engine yields either a finite-panel irrationality statement or a dimension lower bound.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: The source combines Lemmas 1 and 6 in the condition −bϖ_c+2(a+b−1)+κ<0 to conclude that at least one odd ζ(s) with b<s<a+b is irrational, then lists parameter choices for the finite panels. For b=1 it invokes a linear-independence criterion to bound δ(a) using κ, the coefficient-growth rate, and the denominator saving, and selects further parameters to obtain the stated finite and asymptotic dimension results.
directed.conceptual_reading: The strict inequality is a feasibility test for the whole construction: analytic smallness must outrun the arithmetic normalization cost, while dimension estimates additionally account for coefficient growth. Parameter selection simultaneously tunes support and these competing rates.
directed.representation_or_bridge: A scalar inequality aggregates the preceding p-adic and saddle outputs and feeds them into irrationality or linear-independence criteria; choosing a, b, and c maps that abstract feasibility region to concrete zeta panels and dimension bounds.
directed.boundary_or_failure: The conclusions are collective: they do not identify which zeta value in a panel is irrational. The cited independence criterion and several direct or numerical parameter checks are invoked rather than established in this span, so the unit should not be read as a self-contained proof.
